Existence result for degenerate cross-diffusion system with application to seawater intrusion

Jana Alkhayal Affiliation: LaMA-Liban, lebanese university, P.O. Box 37 Tripoli, Lebanon. Email: jana.khayal@hotmail.com Affiliation: Samar Issa Affiliation: LaMA-Liban, lebanese university, P.O. Box 37 Tripoli, Lebanon. Email: samar_issa@live.com Affiliation: Mustapha Jazar Affiliation: LaMA-Liban, lebanese university, P.O. Box 37 Tripoli, Lebanon. Email: mjazar@laser-lb.org Affiliation: Régis Monneau Affiliation: Université Paris-Est, CERMICS, Ecole des Ponts ParisTech, Affiliation: 6 et 8 avenue Blaise Pascal, Cité Descartes Champs-sur-Marne, Affiliation: 77455 Marne-la-vallée Cedex 2, France. Email: monneau@cermics.enpc.fr
Abstract

In this paper, we study degenerate parabolic system, which is strongly coupled. We prove general existence result, but the uniqueness remains an open question. Our proof of existence is based on a crucial entropy estimate which both control the gradient of the solution and the non-negativity of the solution. Our system are of porous medium type and our method applies to models in seawater intrusion.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 35K55, 35K65

Keywords: Degenerate parabolic system; entropy estimate; porous medium like systems.

1 Introduction

For the sake of simplicity, we will work on the torus Ω:=𝕋N=(ℝ/ℤ)N\Omega:=\mathbb{T}^{N}=\left(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\right)^{N}, with N≥1N\geq 1.
Let ΩT:=(0,T)×Ω\Omega_{T}:=(0,T)\times\Omega with T>0T>0. Let an integer m≥1m\geq 1. Our purpose is to study a class of degenerate strongly coupled parabolic system of the form

uti=div(ui∑j=1𝑚Ai​j∇uj) in ΩT, for i=1,…,m.u_{t}^{i}={\rm div}\left(u^{i}\overset{m}{\underset{j=1}{\sum}}A_{ij}\nabla u^{j}\right)\quad\quad\mbox{ in }\Omega_{T},\quad\mbox{ for }i=1,\ldots,m. (1.1)

with the initial condition

ui​(0,x)=u0i​(x)≥0 a.e. in ​Ω, for ​i=1,…,m.u^{i}(0,x)=u^{i}_{0}(x)\geq 0\quad\quad\mbox{ a.e. in }\Omega,\quad\mbox{ for }i=1,\ldots,m. (1.2)

In the core of the paper we will assume that A=(Ai​j)1≤i,j≤mA=(A_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq m} is a real m×mm\times m matrix (not necessarily symmetric) that satisfies the following positivity condition: we assume that there exists δ0>0\delta_{0}>0, such that we have

ξT​A​ξ≥δ0​|ξ|2, for all ​ξ∈ℝm.\xi^{T}A\,\xi\geq\delta_{0}|\xi|^{2},\quad\mbox{ for all }\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (1.3)

This condition can be weaken: see Subsection 4.1. Problem (1.1) appears naturally in the modeling of seawater intrusion (see Subsection 1.2).

1.1 Main results

To introduce our main result, we need to define the nonnegative entropy function Ψ\Psi:

Ψ⁡(a)−1e={a​ln⁡a fora>0,0 fora=0,+∞ fora<0,\displaystyle\Psi(a)-\frac{1}{e}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}a\ln a&\mbox{ for}\quad a>0,\\ 0&\mbox{ for}\quad a=0,\\ +\infty&\mbox{ for}\quad a<0,\end{array}\right.

which is minimal for a=1e\displaystyle a=\frac{1}{e}.

Theorem 1.1.

(Existence for system (1.1))
Assume that AA satisfies (1.3). For i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m, let u0i≥0u_{0}^{i}\geq 0 in Ω\Omega satisfying

∑i=1m∫ΩΨ⁡(u0i)<+∞,\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\Omega}\Psi(u_{0}^{i})<+\infty, (1.8)

where Ψ\Psi is given in (1.1). Then there exists a function u=(ui)1≤i≤m∈(L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))∩C⁡([0,T),(W1,∞​(Ω))′))mu=(u^{i})_{1\leq i\leq m}\in(L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega))\ \cap\ C([0,T);(W^{1,\infty}(\Omega))^{\prime}))^{m} solution in the sense of distributions of (1.1),(1.2), with ui≥0u^{i}\geq 0 a.e. in ΩT\Omega_{T}, for i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. Moreover this solution satisfies the following entropy estimate for a.e. t1,t2∈(0,T)t_{1},t_{2}\in(0,T), with ui​(t2)=ui​(t2,⋅)u^{i}(t_{2})=u^{i}(t_{2},\cdot):

∑i=1m∫ΩΨ⁡(ui​(t2))+δ0​∑i=1m∫t1t2∫Ω|∇ui|2≤∑i=1m∫ΩΨ⁡(u0i),\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\Omega}\Psi(u^{i}(t_{2}))+\delta_{0}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u^{i}|^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\Omega}\Psi(u_{0}^{i}), (1.9)

where Ψ\Psi is given in (1.1).

Here ‖A‖\left\|A\right\| is the matrix norm defined as

‖A‖=sup|ξ|=1|A​ξ|.\left\|A\right\|=\sup_{\left|\xi\right|=1}\left|A\xi\right|. (1.10)

Notice that the entropy estimate (1.9) guarantees that ∇ui∈L2​(0,T,L2​(Ω))\nabla u^{i}\in L^{2}(0,T;L^{2}(\Omega)), and therefore allows us to define the product ui∑i=1mAi​j∇uj\displaystyle u^{i}\sum_{i=1}^{m}A_{ij}\nabla u^{j} in (1.1). When our proofs were obtained, we realized that a similar entropy estimate has been obtained in [7] and [9] for a special system different from ours.

Remark 1.2.

(Decreasing energy)
If AA is a symmetric matrix then a solution uu of system (1.1) satisfies

dd​t(∑i=1m∑j=1m∫Ω12Ai​juiuj)=−∑i=1m∫Ωui|∑j=1mAi​j∇uj|2.\frac{d}{dt}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}A_{ij}u^{i}u^{j}\right)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\Omega}u^{i}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{ij}\nabla u^{j}\right|^{2}.

1.2 Application to seawater intrusion

In this subsection, we describe briefly a model of seawater intrusion, which is particular case of our system (1.1).
An aquifer is an underground layer of a porous and permeable rock through which water can move. On the one hand coastal aquifers contain freshwater and on the other hand saltwater from the sea can enter in the ground and replace the freshwater. We refer to [4] for a general overview on seawater intrusion models.
Now let ν=1−ϵ0∈(0,1)\nu=1-\epsilon_{0}\in(0,1) where

ϵ0=γs−γfγs\epsilon_{0}=\frac{\gamma_{s}-\gamma_{f}}{\gamma_{s}}

with γs\gamma_{s} and γf\gamma_{f} are the specific weight of the saltwater and freshwater respectively.

We assume that in the porous medium, the interface between the saltwater and the bedrock is given as {z=0}\{z=0\}, the interface between the saltwater and the freshwater, which are assumed to be unmiscible, can be written as {z=g(t,x)}\left\{z=g(t,x)\right\}, and the interface between the freshwater and the dry soil can be written as {z=h(t,x)+g(t,x)}\left\{z=h(t,x)+g(t,x)\right\}. Then the evolutions of hh and gg are given by a coupled nonlinear parabolic system (we refer to see [17]) of the form

{ht=div{h∇(ν(h+g))} in ​ΩT,gt=div{g∇(νh+g)} in ​ΩT,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}h_{t}&=&{\rm div}\left\{h\nabla(\nu(h+g))\right\}&\mbox{ in }\Omega_{T},\\ g_{t}&=&{\rm div}\left\{g\nabla(\nu h+g)\right\}&\mbox{ in }\Omega_{T},\\ \end{array}\right.

This is a particular case of (1.1), where the 2×22\times 2 matrix

A=(ννν1)A=\begin{pmatrix}\nu&\nu\\ \nu&1\end{pmatrix} (1.14)

satisfies (1.3).

1.3 Brief review of the litterature

The cross-diffusion systems, in particular the strongly coupled ones (for which the equations are coupled in the highest derivatives terms), are widely presented in different domains such as biology, chemistry, ecology, fluid mechanics and others. They are difficult to treat. Many of the standard results cannot be applied for such problems, such as the maximum principle. Hereafter, we cite several models where our method applies for most of them (see Section 4 for more generalizations on our problem).

In [28], Shigesada, Kawasaki and Teramoto proposed a two-species SKT model in one-dimensional space which arises in population dynamics. It can be written in a generalized form with m-species as

uti−Δ⁡[(βi+∑j=1mαi​j​uj)​ui]=(ai−∑j=1mbi​j​uj)​ui, in ​Ω×(0,T),\displaystyle u_{t}^{i}-\Delta\left[\left(\beta_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{ij}u^{j}\right)u^{i}\right]=\displaystyle\left(a_{i}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_{ij}u^{j}\right)u^{i},\quad\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T), (1.15)

where uiu^{i}, for i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m, denotes the population density of the i-th species and βi\beta_{i}, αi​j\alpha_{ij}, aia_{i}, bi​jb_{ij} are nonnegative constants. The existence of a global solution for such problem in arbitrary space dimension is studied in [32], where the quadratic form of the diffusion matrix is supposed positive definite. On the other hand, the two-species case was frequently studied, see for instance [23, 16, 31, 14, 29] for dimensions 11, 22, and [7, 26, 27, 6] for arbitrary dimension and appropriate conditions.

Another example of such problems is the electochemistry model studied by Choi, Huan and Lui in [8] where they consider the general form

uti=∑ℓ=1n∑j=1m∂∂xℓ(aℓi​j(u)∂uj∂xℓ),u=(ui)1≤i≤mfori=1,…,m,u^{i}_{t}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{\ell}}\left(a^{ij}_{\ell}(u)\frac{\partial u^{j}}{\partial x_{\ell}}\right),\quad u=(u^{i})_{1\leq i\leq m}\quad\mbox{for}\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (1.16)

and prove the existence of a weak solution of (1.16) under assumptions on the matrices Al​(u)=(ali​j​(u))1≤i,j≤mA_{l}(u)=(a_{l}^{ij}(u))_{1\leq i,j\leq m}: it is continuous in uu, its components are uniformly bounded with respect to uu and its symmetric part is definite positive. Their strategy of proof seeks to use Galerkin method to prove the existence of solutions to the linearized system and then to apply Schauder fixed-point theorem. Then they apply the results obtained to an electrochemistry model.

A third example of cross-diffusion models is the chemotaxis model introduced in [20]. The global existence for classical solutions of this model is studied by Hillen and Painter in [15] where they considered

{ut=∇⋅(∇u−χ(u,v)∇v),t>0,x∈Ωvt=μ​Δ​v+g⁡(u,v),t>0,x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{clll}u_{t}&=&\nabla\cdot(\nabla u-\chi(u,v)\nabla v),&\quad t>0,x\in\Omega\\ v_{t}&=&\mu\Delta v+g(u,v),&\quad t>0,x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

on a C3C^{3}- differentiable compact Riemannian manifold without boundary, where the function uu describes the particle density, vv is the density of the external signal, the chemotactic cross-diffusion χ\chi is assumed to be bounded, and the function gg describes production and degradation of the external stimulus. Another kind of chemotaxis model (the angiogenesis system) has been suggested and studied in [9]:

{ut=κΔu−∇⋅(uχ(v)∇v),t>0,x∈Ωvt=−vm​u,t>0,x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{clll}u_{t}&=&\kappa\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\,\chi(v)\nabla v),&\quad t>0,x\in\Omega\\ v_{t}&=&-v^{m}u,&\quad t>0,x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where m≥1m\geq 1 and κ\kappa is a constant.

Moreover, Alt and Luckhaus prove the existence in finite time of a solution for the following elliptic-parabolic problem

∂tbi​(u)−div​(ai​(b⁡(u),∇u))=fi​(b⁡(u)), in ​Ω×(0,T),\partial_{t}b^{i}(u)-\hbox{div}(a^{i}(b(u),\nabla u))=f^{i}(b(u)),\quad\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T), (1.19)

where Ω⊂RN\Omega\subset R^{N} is open, bounded, and connected with Lipschitz boundary, bb is monotone and continuous gradient and aa is continuous and elliptic with some growth condition. This problem can be seen as a standard parabolic equation when b⁡(z)=zb(z)=z.

Another problem is the Muskat Problem for Thin Fluid Layers of the form

{∂tf=(1+R)​∂x(f​∂xf)+R​∂x(f​∂xg),∂tg=Rμ​∂x(g​∂xf)+Rμ​∂x(g​∂xg).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{cll}\partial_{t}f&=&(1+R)\partial_{x}(f\partial_{x}f)+R\partial_{x}(f\partial_{x}g),\\ \partial_{t}g&=&R_{\mu}\partial_{x}(g\partial_{x}f)+R_{\mu}\partial_{x}(g\partial_{x}g).\\ \end{array}\right.

It models, [11], the motion of two fluids with different densities and viscosities in a porous meduim in one dimension, where ff and gg are the thickness of the two fluids and RR, Rμ>0R_{\mu}>0 depending on the densities and the viscosities of the fluids. The authors in [11, 12] studied the classical solutions of such problem. Moreover, weak solutions are established under different assumptions in [10, 24, 18, 19].

1.4 Strategy of the proof

In (1.1), the elliptic part of the equation does not have a Lax-Milgram structure. Otherwise, our existence result is mainly based on the entropy estimate (1.9). It is difficult to get this entropy estimate directly (we do not have enough regularity to do it), so we proceed by approximations.
Approximation 1:
We discretize in time system (1.1), with a time step Δ​t=T/K\Delta t=T/K, where K∈ℕ∗K\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Then for a given un=(ui,n)1≤i≤m∈(H1​(Ω))mu^{n}=(u^{i,n})_{1\leq i\leq m}\in(H^{1}(\Omega))^{m}, we consider the implicit scheme which is an elliptic system:

ui,n+1−ui,nΔ​t=div{ui,n+1∑j=1mAi​j∇uj,n+1}.\displaystyle{\frac{u^{i,n+1}-u^{i,n}}{\Delta t}}={\rm div}\left\{u^{i,n+1}\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{ij}\nabla u^{j,n+1}\right\}. (1.21)

Approximation 2:
We regularize the right-hand term of (1.21). To do that, we take η>0\eta>0 and 0<ϵ<1<ℓ0<\epsilon<1<\ell, and we choose the following regularization

ui,n+1−ui,nΔ​t=div{Tϵ,ℓ(ui,n+1)∑j=1mAi​j∇ρη⋆ρη⋆uj,n+1},\displaystyle{\frac{u^{i,n+1}-u^{i,n}}{\Delta t}}={\rm div}\left\{T^{\epsilon,\ell}(u^{i,n+1})\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{ij}\nabla\rho_{\eta}\star\rho_{\eta}\star u^{j,n+1}\right\}, (1.22)

where Tϵ,ℓT^{\epsilon,\ell} is truncation operator defined as

Tϵ,ℓ​(a):={ϵ if ​a≤ϵ,a if ​ϵ≤a≤ℓ,ℓ if ​a≥ℓ,\displaystyle T^{\epsilon,\ell}(a):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cll}\epsilon&\mbox{ if }a\leq\epsilon,\\ a&\mbox{ if }\epsilon\leq a\leq\ell,\\ \ell&\mbox{ if }a\geq\ell,\end{array}\right.

and the mollifier ρη​(x)=η−N​ρ​(x/η)\rho_{\eta}(x)=\eta^{-N}\rho\left(x/\eta\right) with ρ∈Cc∞​(ℝN)\rho\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{N}), ρ≥0\rho\geq 0, ∫ℝNρ=1\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}\rho=1 and ρ⁡(−x)=ρ⁡(x)\rho(-x)=\rho(x).
Now, with the convolution by ρη\rho_{\eta} in (1.22), the term ∇ρη⋆ρη⋆uj,n+1\nabla\rho_{\eta}\star\rho_{\eta}\star u^{j,n+1} behaves like uj,n+1u^{j,n+1}.
Note that, considering the ℤN\mathbb{Z}^{N}- periodic extension on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} of uj,n+1u^{j,n+1}, the convolution ρη⋆uj,n+1\rho_{\eta}\star u^{j,n+1} is possible over ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}.
Approximation 3:
Let δ>0\delta>0. We will add a second order term like δ​Δ​ui\delta\Delta u^{i} to equation (1.22) in order to obtain an elliptic one. More specifically, we consider div(δTϵ,ℓ(ui)∇ui){\rm div}\left(\delta T^{\epsilon,\ell}(u^{i})\nabla u^{i}\right) instead of δ​Δ​ui\delta\Delta u^{i}, to keep an entropy estimate.
Then we freeze the coefficients ui,n+1u^{i,n+1} on the right-hand side to make a linear structure (these coefficients are now called δ​Tϵ,ℓ​(vi,n+1)\delta T^{\epsilon,\ell}(v^{i,n+1})), we obtain the following modified system:

ui,n+1−ui,nΔ​t=div{Tϵ,ℓ(vi,n+1)(∑j=1𝑚Ai​j∇ρη⋆ρη⋆uj,n+1+δ∇ui,n+1)}.\displaystyle{\frac{u^{i,n+1}-u^{i,n}}{\Delta t}}={\rm div}\left\{T^{\epsilon,\ell}(v^{i,n+1})\left(\overset{m}{\underset{j=1}{\sum}}A_{ij}\nabla\rho_{\eta}\star\rho_{\eta}\star u^{j,n+1}+\delta\nabla u^{i,n+1}\right)\right\}. (1.27)

We will look for fixed points solutions vi,n+1=ui,n+1v^{i,n+1}=u^{i,n+1} of this modified system. Finally, we will recover the expected result dropping one after one all the approximations.

1.5 Organization of the paper

In Section 2, we recall some useful tools. In Section 3, we study system (1.1). By discretizing our problem on time, in Subsection 3.1, we obtain an elliptic problem. We use the Lax-Milgram theorem to show the existence of a unique solution to the linear problem (1.27). We demonstrate, in Subsection 3.2, the existence of a solution of the nonlinear problem, using the Schaefer’s fixed point theorem.
Then we pass to the limit in the following order: (Δ​t,ϵ)→(0,0)(\Delta t,\epsilon)\rightarrow(0,0) in Subsection 3.3, (ℓ,η)→(∞,0)(\ell,\eta)\rightarrow(\infty,0) in Subsection 3.4 and δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0 in Subsection 3.5. Generalizations (including more general matrices AA or tensors) will be presented in Section 4. We end with an Appendix showing some technical results in Section 5.

2 Preliminary tools

Theorem 2.1.

(Schaefer’s fixed point theorem)[13, Theorem 4 page 504]
Let XX be a real Banach space. Suppose that

Φ:X→X\Phi:X\to X

is a continuous and compact mapping. Assume further that the set

{u∈X,u=λΦ(u)for someλ∈[0,1]}\left\{u\in X,\quad u=\lambda\Phi(u)\quad\mbox{for some}\quad\lambda\in[0,1]\right\}

is bounded. Then Φ\Phi has a fixed point.

Proposition 2.2.

(Aubin’s lemma)[30]
For any T>0T>0, and Ω=𝕋N\Omega=\mathbb{T}^{N}, let EE denote the space

E:={g∈L2((0,T);H1(Ω)) and gt∈L2((0,T);H−1(Ω))},E:=\left\{g\in L^{2}((0,T);H^{1}(\Omega))\mbox{ and }g_{t}\in L^{2}((0,T);H^{-1}(\Omega))\right\},

endowed with the Hilbert norm

‖ω‖E=(‖ω‖L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))2+‖ωt‖L2​(0,T,H−1​(Ω))2)12.\left\|\omega\right\|_{E}=\left(\left\|\omega\right\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega))}+\left\|\omega_{t}\right\|^{2}_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-1}(\Omega))}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

The embedding

E↪L2​((0,T),L2​(Ω))is compact.E\hookrightarrow L^{2}((0,T);L^{2}(\Omega))\quad\mbox{is compact.}

On the other hand, it follows from [21, Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 3.1, Chapter 1] that the embedding

E↪C⁡([0,T],L2​(Ω))is continuous.E\hookrightarrow C([0,T];L^{2}(\Omega))\quad\mbox{is continuous}.
Lemma 2.3.

(Simon’s Lemma)[30]
Let XX, BB and YY three Banach spaces, where X↪BX\hookrightarrow B with compact embedding and B↪YB\hookrightarrow Y with continuous embedding. If (gn)n(g^{n})_{n} is a sequence such that

‖gn‖Lq​(0,T,B)+‖gn‖L1​(0,T,X)+‖gtn‖L1​(0,T,Y)≤C,\|g^{n}\|_{L^{q}(0,T;B)}+\|g^{n}\|_{L^{1}(0,T;X)}+\|g_{t}^{n}\|_{L^{1}(0,T;Y)}\leq C,

where 1<q≤∞1<q\leq\infty, and CC is a constant independent of nn, then (gn)n(g^{n})_{n} is relatively compact in Lp​(0,T,B)L^{p}(0,T;B) for all 1≤p<q1\leq p<q.

Now we will present the variant of the original result of Simon’s lemma [30, Corollary 6, page 87]. First of all, let us define the norm ‖.‖Var​([a,b),Y)\left\|.\right\|_{\mbox{Var}([a,b);Y)} where YY is a Banach space with the norm ‖.‖Y\left\|.\right\|_{Y}.
For a function g:[a,b)→Yg:[a,b)\to Y, we set

‖g‖Var​([a,b),Y)=sup∑j‖g⁡(aj+1)−g⁡(aj)‖Y\left\|g\right\|_{\mbox{Var}([a,b);Y)}=\sup\sum_{j}\left\|g(a_{j+1})-g(a_{j})\right\|_{Y} (2.1)

over all possible finite partitions:

a≤a0<⋯<ak<ba\leq a_{0}<\dots<a_{k}<b
Theorem 2.4.

(Variant of Simon’s Lemma)
Let XX, BB and YY three Banach spaces, where X↪BX\hookrightarrow B with compact embedding and B↪YB\hookrightarrow Y with continuous embedding. Let (gn)n(g^{n})_{n} be a sequence such that

‖gn‖L1​(0,T,X)+‖gn‖Lq​(0,T,B)+‖gn‖Var​([0,T),Y)≤C,\left\|g^{n}\right\|_{L^{1}(0,T;X)}+\left\|g^{n}\right\|_{L^{q}(0,T;B)}+\left\|g^{n}\right\|_{\mbox{Var}([0,T);Y)}\leq C, (2.2)

where 1<q<∞1<q<\infty, and CC is a constant independent of nn. Then (gn)n(g^{n})_{n} is relatively compact in Lp​(0,T,B)L^{p}(0,T;B) for all 1≤p<q1\leq p<q.

Proof.

Step 1: Regularization of the sequence
Let ρ¯∈Cc∞​(ℝ)\bar{\rho}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}) with ρ¯≥0\bar{\rho}\geq 0, ∫ℝρ¯=1\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bar{\rho}=1 and supp​ρ¯⊂(−1,1)\mbox{supp}\ \bar{\rho}\subset(-1,1). For ε>0\varepsilon>0, we set

ρ¯ε​(x)=ε−1​ρ¯​(ε−1​x).\bar{\rho}_{\varepsilon}(x)=\varepsilon^{-1}\bar{\rho}(\varepsilon^{-1}x).

We extend gn=gn​(t)g^{n}=g^{n}(t) by zero outside the time interval [0,T)[0,T). Because q<+∞q<+\infty, we see that for each nn, we choose some 0<εn→00<\varepsilon_{n}\to 0 as n→+∞n\to+\infty such that

‖g¯n−gn‖Lq​(0,T,B)→0asn→+∞,withg¯n=ρ¯εn⋆gn\left\|\bar{g}^{n}-g^{n}\right\|_{L^{q}(0,T;B)}\rightarrow 0\quad\mbox{as}\quad n\to+\infty,\quad\mbox{with}\quad\bar{g}^{n}=\bar{\rho}_{\varepsilon_{n}}\star g^{n} (2.3)

and

Step 2: Checking (2.4)
By (2.2) there exists a sequence of step functions fηf_{\eta} which approximates uniformly gng^{n} on [0,T)[0,T) as η→0\eta\to 0, with moreover satisfies

Therefore we get easily (for εn<δ\varepsilon_{n}<\delta)

‖(ρ¯εn⋆fη)t‖L1​(δ,T−δ,Y)≤‖fη‖Var​([0,T),Y)\left\|(\bar{\rho}_{\varepsilon_{n}}\star f_{\eta})_{t}\right\|_{L^{1}(\delta,T-\delta;Y)}\leq\left\|f_{\eta}\right\|_{\mbox{Var}([0,T);Y)}

which implies (2.4), when we pass to the limit as η\eta goes to zero.
Step 3: Conclusion
We can then apply Corollary 6 in [30] to deduce that g¯n\bar{g}^{n} is relatively compact in Lp​(0,T,B)L^{p}(0,T;B) for all 1≤p<q1\leq p<q. Because of (2.3), we deduce that this is also the case for the sequence (gn)n(g^{n})_{n}, which ends the proof of the Theorem. ∎

3 Existence for system (1.1)

Our goal is to prove Theorem 1.1 in order to get the existence of a solution for system (1.1).

Remark 3.4.

(Another method following [21])
Note that it would be also possible to use a theorem in Lions-Magenes [21, Chap. 3, Theorem 4.1, page 257]. This would prove in particular the existence of a unique solution for the following system:

{uti=div⁡{Jϵ,ℓ,η,δi​(v,u)} in𝒟′​(ΩT),Jϵ,ℓ,η,δi​(v,u)=Tϵ,ℓ(vi){∑j=1𝑚Ai​j∇ρη⋆ρη⋆uj+δ∇ui},ui​(0,x)=u0i​(x) in Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{clll}\displaystyle{u^{i}_{t}}&=&{\rm div}\left\{J_{\epsilon,\ell,\eta,\delta}^{i}(v,u)\right\}&\quad\mbox{ in}\quad{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}(\Omega_{T}),\\ J_{\epsilon,\ell,\eta,\delta}^{i}(v,u)&=&T^{\epsilon,\ell}(v^{i})\left\{\overset{m}{\underset{j=1}{\sum}}A_{ij}\nabla\rho_{\eta}\star\rho_{\eta}\star u^{j}+\delta\nabla u^{i}\right\},&\\ u^{i}(0,x)&=&u^{i}_{0}(x)&\quad\mbox{ in }\quad\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where Tϵ,ℓT^{\epsilon,\ell} is given in (1.4).
It would then be possible to find a fixed point solution v=uv=u of (3.4) to recover a solution of (3.3). We would have to justify again the entropy inequality (3.38).

Assumption (1.3) can be weaken. Indead, we can assume that A=(Ai​j)1≤i,j≤mA=(A_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq m} is a real m×mm\times m matrix that satisfies a positivity condition, in the sense that there exist two positive definite diagonal m×mm\times m matrices LL and RR and δ0>0\delta_{0}>0, such that we have

ζT​L​A​R​ζ≥δ0​|ζ|2,for allζ∈ℝm.\zeta^{T}LAR\,\zeta\geq\delta_{0}|\zeta|^{2},\quad\mbox{for all}\quad\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (4.1)

The assumption of positivity condition (4.1), generalize our problem for AA not necessarily having a symmetric part positive definite. Here is an example of such a matrix, whose symmetric part is not definite positive, but the symmetric part of L​A​RL\,A\,R is definite positive for some suitable positive diagonal matrices LL and RR.
We consider

A=(1−a2​a1)​with ​|a|>2.A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-a\\ 2a&1\end{pmatrix}\mbox{with }\left|a\right|>2.

Indeed,

satisfying det(As​y​m)=1−a24<0\displaystyle\det(A^{sym})=1-\frac{a^{2}}{4}<0. And let

L=(2001)andR=I2=(1001).L=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}\quad\mbox{and}\quad R=I_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}.

On the other hand,

B=L.A.R=(2−2​a2​a1),B=L.A.R=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2a\\ 2a&1\end{pmatrix},

satisfies that

Bs​y​m=(2001),B^{sym}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix},

is definite positive.

Our study can be applied on a generalized systems of the form

uti=∑j=1m∑k=1N∑l=1N∂∂xk​(fi​(ui)​Ai​j​k​l​∂uj∂xl) for ​i=1,…,m,u^{i}_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{l=1}^{N}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{k}}\left(f_{i}(u^{i})A_{ijkl}\frac{\partial u^{j}}{\partial x_{l}}\right)\quad\mbox{ for }i=1,\ldots,m, (4.2)

where fif_{i} satisfies

{fi∈C⁡(ℝ),0≤fi​(a)≤C⁡(1+|a|) for ​a∈ℝ​ and ​C>0,c​|a|≤fi​(a) for ​a∈[0,a0]with ​a0,c>0,∫a0A1fi​(a)​da<+∞ for all ​A≥a0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}f_{i}\in C(\mathbb{R}),&\\ \\ 0\leq f_{i}(a)\leq{C}(1+|a|)&{\quad\mbox{ for }a\in\mathbb{R}\mbox{ and }C>0,}\\ \\ {c\left|a\right|\leq}f_{i}(a)&\quad\mbox{ for }a\in[0,a_{0}]\quad\mbox{with }a_{0},c>0,\\ \\ \displaystyle\int_{a_{0}}^{A}\frac{1}{f_{i}(a)}\,da<+\infty&\quad\mbox{ for all }A\geq a_{0}.\end{array}\right.

An example for such fif_{i} is

fi​(a)=max⁡(0,min⁡(a,|a−1|)).f_{i}(a)=\max\left(0,\min\left(a,\sqrt{\left|a-1\right|}\right)\right).

Moreover, A=(Ai​j​k​l)i,j,k,lA=(A_{ijkl})_{i,j,k,l} is a tensor of order 4 that satisfies the following positivity condition: there exists δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 such that

∑i,j,k,lAi​j​k​l​ηi​ηj​ζk​ζl≥δ0​|η|2​|ζ|2 for all ​η∈ℝm,ζ∈ℝN.\sum_{i,j,k,l}A_{ijkl}\,\eta^{i}\,\eta^{j}\,\zeta_{k}\,\zeta_{l}\,\geq\delta_{0}|\eta|^{2}|\zeta|^{2}\quad\mbox{ for all }\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. (4.4)

Here the coefficients Ai​j​(x,u)A_{ij}(x,u) may depend continuously of (x,u)(x,u). uti=div(ui∑j=1mAi​j(x,u)∇u)+gi(x,u),with gi≥0,u^{i}_{t}={\rm div}\left(u^{i}\sum_{j=1}^{m}A_{ij}(x,u)\nabla u\right)+g^{i}(x,u),\quad\mbox{with }g^{i}\geq 0,

Moreover, our method applies to models of the form

We can consider the model

5 Appendix: Technical results

In this section we will present some technical results that are used in our proofs.

Proposition 5.1.

(Recovering the initial condition)
Let Y be a Banach space with the norm ‖.‖Y\left\|.\right\|_{Y}. Consider a sequence (gm)m∈C⁡(0,T,Y)(g_{m})_{m}\in C(0,T;Y) such that (gm)t(g_{m})_{t} is uniformly bounded in Lq​(0,T,Y)L^{q}(0,T;Y) with 1<q≤∞1<q\leq\infty, and (gm)|t=0→g0(g_{m})_{|t=0}\rightarrow g_{0} in YY. Then there exists g∈C⁡(0,T,Y)g\in C(0,T;Y) such that gm→gg_{m}\rightarrow g in C⁡(0,T,Y)C(0,T;Y) and

g|t=0=g0in Y.g_{|t=0}=g_{0}\qquad\mbox{in }Y.
Proof.

We have that for all s<t∈(0,T)s<t\in(0,T)

‖gm​(t)−gm​(s)‖Y\displaystyle\|g_{m}(t)-g_{m}(s)\|_{Y} =\displaystyle= ‖∫st(gm)τ​(τ)‖Y\displaystyle\left\|\int_{s}^{t}(g_{m})_{\tau}(\tau)\right\|_{Y} (5.1)
≤\displaystyle\leq ∫st‖(gm)τ​(τ)‖Y​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{s}^{t}\|(g_{m})_{\tau}(\tau)\|_{Y}\;ds
≤\displaystyle\leq (t−s)q−1q​‖(gm)τ​(τ)‖Lq​(0,T,Y)≤(t−s)q−1q​C,\displaystyle(t-s)^{\frac{q-1}{q}}\;\|(g_{m})_{\tau}(\tau)\|_{L^{q}(0,T;Y)}\leq(t-s)^{\frac{q-1}{q}}C,

where we have used in the second line Holder’s inequality, and the fact that (gm)τ(g_{m})_{\tau} is uniformly bounded in Lq​(0,T,Y)L^{q}(0,T;Y). Since (5.1) implies the equicontinuity of (gm)m(g_{m})_{m}, by Arzelà-Ascoli theorem, there exists g∈C⁡(0,T,Y)g\in C(0,T;Y) such that gm→gg_{m}\rightarrow g in C⁡(0,T,Y)C(0,T;Y). Moreover, Taking s=0s=0 in (5.1) we get

‖gm​(t)−gm​(0)‖Y≤tq−1q​C.\|g_{m}(t)-g_{m}(0)\|_{Y}\leq t^{\frac{q-1}{q}}C. (5.2)

By passing to the limit in mm in (5.2), we deduce that

‖g⁡(t)−g0‖Y≤tq−1q​C\displaystyle\|g(t)-g_{0}\|_{Y}\leq t^{\frac{q-1}{q}}C

Particularly, for t=0t=0, we have

‖g⁡(0)−g0‖Y=0.\displaystyle\|g(0)-g_{0}\|_{Y}=0.

This implies the result. ∎

Lemma 5.2.

(Convergence result)
Let (aϵ)ϵ(a_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon} a real sequence such that aϵ→a0a_{\epsilon}\rightarrow a_{0} as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0. Then we have

Ψ0,ℓ​(a0)≤lim infϵ→0Ψϵ,ℓ​(aϵ),\Psi_{0,\ell}(a_{0})\leq\liminf_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0}\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell}(a_{\epsilon}),

where Ψϵ,ℓ\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell} and Ψ0,ℓ{\Psi_{0,\ell}} are given in (3.2) and (3.3) respectively.

Proof.

Consider the case where a0=0a_{0}=0.
We suppose that the sequence (aϵ)ϵ∈(−∞;1e](a_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon}\in(-\infty;\frac{1}{e}]. Let (bϵ)ϵ∈(−∞;1e](b_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon}\in(-\infty;\frac{1}{e}] a sequence that decreases to 00 as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 with bϵ>aϵb_{\epsilon}>a_{\epsilon}. Since Ψϵ,ℓ\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell} is decreasing on (−∞;1e](-\infty;\frac{1}{e}] we have Ψϵ,ℓ​(aϵ)≥Ψϵ,ℓ​(bϵ)\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell}(a_{\epsilon})\geq\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell}(b_{\epsilon}). Moreover, using the fact that Ψϵ,ℓ​(bϵ)→0=Ψ0,ℓ​(0)\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell}(b_{\epsilon})\rightarrow 0=\Psi_{0,\ell}(0) we get the result.
Otherwise, when (aϵ)ϵ∈(1e,+∞)(a_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon}\in(\frac{1}{e};+\infty) the proof is the same as above but with taking bϵ<aϵb_{\epsilon}<a_{\epsilon} since Ψϵ,ℓ\Psi_{\epsilon,\ell} is nondecreasing in (1e,+∞)(\frac{1}{e};+\infty).
For the other cases, a0<0a_{0}<0 and a0>0a_{0}>0, the result is easily obtained. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
